thread_title: Pruning progress (photos!) and winter care,  Jan. 2014
breadcrumb: Pruning progress (photos!) and winter care,  Jan. 2014

posts.body_html:
Normally, when it's freezing cold outside, I'm not as worried about pruning, pests, rot, and diseases. However, with the warm temperatures and extreme drought we've been having here in California, we have new challenges that are othewise normally "dormant". First off, there's potentially less time to prune and transplant because we are in danger of having the plants break out of dormancy earlier than normal. Another challenge are pests, like thrips and mealy bugs. With warmer temperatures comes bigger winter pest populations, and controlling them early in the season is crucial to prevent outbreaks and crop damage.



Sanitation and prevention are the best ways to keep your plants healthy. Clear up all the weeds in the surrounding area to prevent overwintering pests from having a "hide out" during the dormancy period. Cut away all dead pitchers and get those rhizomes exposed to light-this will help ward off fungi and bacterial issues.

Here's a photo of a tub of S. leucophylla Hurricane creek white before being pruned. Had I left these pitchers on for a few more weeks, a couple of these rhizomes may have rotted out, as this dense layer of leaves creates a humid, dark microclimate, which invites many nasty fungi and bacteria to attack:




Here's the same tub, but now it's all cleaned up. Bacteria and fungi have a harder time attacking the rhizomes under this circumstance because there's a lot better air flow, and the sun dries out the surface:


I'm not too worried about the S. roseas-they don't seem to need as much care during the winter, but they will benefit from cleaning up the dead leaves. I haven't gotten to this pot yet:



A little more than half of the collection has been trimmed-still have a ways to go:



Lots of dead leaves:



There are massive piles of leaves:




In the front are plants that still need trimming, whereas in the back, they're all done. Looks a lot cleaner and organized once they're all pruned:



Another shot:



One last one:

posts.body_html:
I have been performing this chore here in Missouri as well. Though the bugs aren't a concern because of the fairly low temps, I still worry about fungal attack. I am actually just starting my second round of trimming. I usually hit them in December first, being sure to only remove dead tissue. Now that it has been a month or two and there is more die back, I am going through again, this time being less judicious and more Freddy Krueger-esk.

On a jealous note: your winter still looks likes summer, Mike! I am totally moving to California. Midwestern winters blow... literally. The wind has been awful here lately.

posts.body_html: Wow, your pictures look so hot (temp. wise). When do you do all your dividing/transplanting?

posts.body_html:
cbennett-that sounds like an ideal pruning method because you keep the maximum amount of green on the plant while minimizing the amount of dead leaf material. If you have the time, it's better than what I do (ie. only go through them once with the pruning shears since it's very time consuming). Indeed, I've been watching your weather the past few weeks, and can only imagine what it's like!


Here in California, I like to have all the pruning done by mid January and all the repotting done by early March. You can start dividing as soon as the plants go dormant around early November, and I've noticed if you divide earlier, they have all winter long to "heal" from the cuts. This allows them to focus their energy on growth as soon as the spring arrives.

posts.body_html:
Mike,

Have you notice any problems with rhizomes rotting to succumbing to Botrytis when you divide in early winter? We debate this every year in our nursery since we had one year where we did have some losses when we divided real early. What seemed to be happening (not sure it this was really the case) is that their freeze resistance was reduced after division. As it is now we now start division in late January, and continue into March since our plants come out of dormancy a bit later than yours.

Jeff

posts.body_html:
Hi Jeff,

Not at all-never had any rot problems caused by dividing early in the dormancy period-in fact, it's been a good preventative measure here, as I'm able to cut out the old, dead material early on before it gets infected and eats up the healthy tissue.

However, you bring up a good point: you and I have completely different winter temperatures. Here, our night temperatures don't usually go below 25F, and are typically around 40-50F during the day, with bright sunshine. Despite being cold, the cumulative exposure to full sun every day probably helps them callus a lot faster too, although light isn't needed for this. There's also very good air circulation. If you have extreme freezing temperatures, it'll theoretically take the rhizomes a lot longer to callus, which could account for lower resistance to mold. You may also cover your plants with black plastic or remay during the extreme cold temperatures, which lowers air circulation and increases relative humidity. On the other hand, freezing cold isn't good for fungal growth either.

That is certainly a great experiment to run, but I'm guessing not every winter will be the same temperature-wise, so it's hard to prove one way or another. I bet a lot of it has to do with the local weather, the botrytis spore "bank" in the soil, and the native concentration of botrytis/pathogen spores in the air at the time of dividing. If you take divisions when the spore population is very high and the temperatures are conducive to pathogens, I would expect a lot of rot issues.

With the previous comments in mind--particilarly the last few relating to spore counts and the like--I wonder if an application of neem or other preventative at the time of division would be a good and/or adequate precaution. I am sure you folks know ofthe cinnamon trick from the orchid world, too. In either case, it should help minimize the efficacy of the spores and the potential foothold for the disease.

*shrugs*. Does anyone take such measures?

posts.body_html:
Merit will not help the Botrytis - Merit is an insecticide.

We suggest Captan fungicide powder on the "open wound" of the division. You can also find it on amazon and it's not expensive. The Captan powder creates a scab covering and protecting the exposed tissue. It is not systemic, but works well. We also mix Captan with water and spray seed trays before they are stratified.

We've had bad results with systemic fungicides.
